summary: Specifies version 1.0 of Datagram Transport Layer Security, which brings TLS-style privacy to datagram protocols such as those running over UDP. It is based on TLS and aims to give equivalent security guarantees while preserving datagram semantics. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 6347.

eli5.summary: TLS locks your messages on connections that never lose a letter. This version does the same for connections that sometimes drop or shuffle letters.

subtitle: TLS adapted to survive lost, reordered and duplicated packets, so datagram applications can be secured too.

tldr.problem: TLS needs a reliable transport such as TCP, so it breaks on datagram traffic where packets can be lost or reordered.
tldr.mechanism: DTLS makes minimal changes to TLS 1.1: explicit epoch and sequence numbers in each record, a stateless cookie exchange, handshake sequence numbers with fragmentation, and retransmission timers.
tldr.outcome: DTLS 1.0 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 6347. It was also updated by RFC 5746 and RFC 7507.

today: DTLS 1.0 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 6347, which is the specification to use. RFC 4347 was also updated by RFC 5746 and RFC 7507.

sections.title: Why TLS Needed a Datagram Version
sections.content:
TLS is widely used to protect Web traffic and email protocols, and it gives applications a transparent connection-oriented channel. But it must run over a reliable transport, typically TCP, so it cannot secure unreliable datagram traffic. More and more applications use UDP, such as the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and electronic gaming protocols.

Designers of those applications had unsatisfactory choices. IPsec suits only some applications, and a custom application layer security protocol takes a large amount of design effort. Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) is deliberately as similar to TLS as possible, to minimize new security invention and maximize code reuse.

DTLS is designed to run in application space without kernel changes. It preserves datagram behavior for payload data: it does not compensate for lost or re-ordered traffic, so media streaming, telephony and gaming behave as before.
sections.eli5: People wanted a lock for fast, careless mail like postcards, but the only lock available needed a careful mail service. DTLS is a lock built for postcards.

sections.title: How DTLS Fixes Unreliability
sections.content:
Unreliability breaks TLS at two levels. First, the TLS record layer does not allow records to be decrypted independently, so if record N is missing, record N+1 cannot be decrypted. Second, the handshake assumes messages arrive reliably and in order.

For records, the fix is borrowed from IPsec ESP: add explicit state. DTLS adds explicit sequence numbers, and TLS 1.1 already adds explicit CBC state. For the handshake, a simple retransmission timer handles loss, a message_seq number per handshake message handles reordering, and fragmentation handles messages bigger than a datagram. Handshake messages can be up to 2^24-1 bytes in theory, while UDP datagrams are often limited to under 1500 bytes.

DTLS optionally supports replay detection using a bitmap window of received records, the same technique as IPsec AH and ESP. It is optional because packet duplication is not always malicious.
sections.eli5: Numbering each page lets the reader sort them even if they arrive jumbled. A timer says when to shout "please send that again".

sections.title: The DTLS Record Layer
sections.content:
The DTLS record layer is TLS 1.1 with one change: a record carries an explicit epoch (16 bits) and sequence_number (48 bits) before its length. DTLS 1.0 uses the on-the-wire version {254, 255}, the 1's complement of the version, so records from TLS and DTLS are easy to tell apart. The epoch is a counter incremented on every cipher state change, and the sequence number is set to zero after each ChangeCipherSpec.

Each record MUST fit within a single datagram, and several records may share a datagram, but a record may not span datagrams. Implementations SHOULD find the MTU and send records smaller than it to avoid IP fragmentation, and handshake messages are sent with the DF bit set. DTLS records carry no association identifiers, so applications must multiplex associations themselves, presumably by host and port with UDP.

The MAC is computed as in TLS 1.1, but over the 64-bit value formed from the epoch and sequence number. A bad MAC need not end the connection: implementations SHOULD silently discard the record. RC4 MUST NOT be used with DTLS. Anti-replay uses a sliding window; a minimum window of 32 MUST be supported and 64 is the preferred default.
sections.eli5: Every sealed envelope gets a counter on the outside. A bad envelope can be thrown away without stopping the whole conversation.

sections.title: The Handshake, Cookies and Retransmission
sections.content:
DTLS uses the TLS handshake messages and flows with three changes: a stateless cookie exchange, a modified handshake header, and retransmission timers. The cookie defends against two attacks: exhausting server resources with handshake requests, and using the server as an amplifier by forging the victim's source address. The server MAY answer a ClientHello with a HelloVerifyRequest (type 3) holding a cookie of up to 32 bytes, and the client MUST resend the ClientHello with it. This does not defend against attacks from valid IP addresses.

A server SHOULD build cookies so they can be checked without per-client state, for example as an HMAC of a secret, the client IP and the client parameters. Servers SHOULD perform the exchange for every new handshake unless amplification is not a problem, and clients MUST be prepared to do it every time.

The handshake header gains message_seq, fragment_offset and fragment_length. Messages are grouped into flights that are retransmitted as a unit. Implementations SHOULD start with a 1 second timer and double it at each retransmission, up to no less than 60 seconds. Alert messages are not retransmitted.
sections.eli5: Before the server does any hard work, it sends a ticket to the address that called. Only someone who really got the ticket can send it back, so fakers are stopped.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
DTLS is a variant of TLS 1.1, so most security considerations are those of TLS 1.1. The main extra concern is denial of service. Servers that skip the cookie exchange are still vulnerable and may be used as attack amplifiers even when they are not themselves under attack, so servers SHOULD use it unless amplification is not a threat in their environment.

DTLS uses the same identifier space as TLS, so no new IANA registries are needed. It adds one new handshake message, hello_verify_request, with value 3. Authors of new TLS identifiers MUST say whether they suit DTLS.
sections.eli5: The biggest danger is someone making the server shout at an innocent victim. The ticket check is what stops that.
